Background:
Vegetation and peat fires are expected to increase under climate extremes [ 1–3 ]. Studies have projected increases in the frequency and intensity of fires in the future [ 1 , 4 ] and the impact on exposed populations could vary by region based on socioeconomic disparities [ 5–7 ]. The severity of fires differs by various factors, including climate, such as the El Niño phenomena [ 8–10 ], vegetation, human activities, and land use [ 2 , 11 ]. Southeast Asia is a region of concern, as different areas within it comprise varying characteristics of the aforementioned factors [ 12 , 13 ]. In previous decades, the region has experienced among the worst fire-related particle exposures [ 5 ].

There are 14.9 million hectares of peatland in Indonesia, of which ∼18% are located in the province of Central Kalimantan [ 14 ], where peat fires are a major air-pollution issue [ 2 , 15 , 16 ]. Peat fire is characterized by its nature of smoldering in the peat layer underground and flaming up under dry and flammable conditions [ 17 ]. Extremely high levels of particulate matter (PM) have been reported due to smoke haze [ 18–20 ] and these affect the air quality regionally. The complicated combination of climate conditions and fire characteristics, such as moisture, temperature, biomass types, and smoldering or flaming types of fires, leads to emissions of different forms and chemical constituents [ 21–25 ]. While several studies have quantified the health impact attributable to smoke haze in Southeast Asia [ 10 , 26 , 27 ], challenges remain in providing epidemiological evidence in this region [ 28 ].

Epidemiological studies have demonstrated adverse health effects associated with exposure to ambient PM [ 29 ], including those caused by different sources and chemical constituents [ 30 ]. Short-term exposure to smoke haze can lead to increased risks in both respiratory mortality [ 31–34 ] and morbidity [ 31 , 35–43 ], but evidence from tropical peatlands remains scarce. Several epidemiological studies in Southeast Asia were conducted in areas located downwind of peat fires during southwest monsoon seasons [ 32 , 43–46 ] and agricultural burning seasons [ 42 ], where increased respiratory hospitalization due to fire-PM was pronounced [ 42 , 43 ]. However, fire intensity might not exactly reflect levels of smoke exposure [ 34 , 45 ]. Detailed studies on smoke haze, with and without considering fire activities, would be beneficial in elucidating the differential impact of different haze conditions.

Previous studies have used smoke-haze indicators [ 32 , 34 , 35 , 45 ], cut-off levels of PM [ 42 , 47 ], air-quality indices [ 46 ], and combinations of several definitions [ 42 , 43 ] to classify a haze day and whether it is affected by local or distant burnings. This may be due to the diverse characteristics of local activities, fires, and smoke from different types of vegetation or land, as well as climate conditions [ 28 ]. Some studies have also reported adverse respiratory effects of fires comprising larger areas [ 34 ] and in the post-fire period [ 41 ]. In addition, the toxicity of components derived from peat fires may differ from those of other vegetation types [ 25 ] and pollutant concentrations can vary by distance [ 18 ] and time since ignition [ 48 ]. This suggests the need to consider fire characteristics and duration when assessing the impact on health.

This study aims to examine the association between smoke haze and respiratory-related visits to primary healthcare centers in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia. Specifically, the effects of haze according to the presence of fire activity, duration of haze, and lag patterns were assessed.
Methods:
### Study settings

Two second-level administrative subdivisions in the province of Central Kalimantan in Indonesia—Palangka Raya City and Pulang Pisau Regency—were investigated ( Fig. 1 ). These subdivisions had populations of 293 457 and 134 499, respectively [ 49 ]. The study period spanned from 2015 to 2019, which included several major smoke-haze episodes in the region.

### Data sources

Health data included daily respiratory visits to public primary healthcare centers—community clinics, known as puskesmas (short for “ Pusat Kesehatan Masyarakat ”) in Central Kalimantan. Handwritten records of visits to puskesmas were transcribed into English and digital forms and aggregated into daily counts. Due to data-collection feasibility, data quality, and data-availability limitations, 18 puskesmas were non-sampled, whereas data from one puskesmas was excluded. Data from six puskesmas were included for analysis. Puskesmas were grouped by subdivision— Puskesmas Kereng Bangkirai, Puskesmas Menteng, and Puskesmas Tangkiling in Palangka Raya City, and Puskesmas Bereng, Puskesmas Bukit Rawi, and Puskesmas Pulang Pisau in Pulang Pisau Regency.

Due to the limitations of ground-measured PM 10 (particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter <10 μm) data, satellite data from Aerosol Robotic Network (AERONET) Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) and Advanced Himawari 8 Imager (AHI) were used to estimate the PM 10 concentrations. PM 10 was estimated by using Equation (1) . However, both cloud and haze can affect AOD values through surface reflectance and aerosol scattering. Therefore, the AOD values were adjusted by incorporating albedo values using Equation (2) ( R 2 =0.91). Details are elaborated in Supplementary Note S1 :

Fire hotspot counts were retrieved from satellite data obtained from MODIS active fire data in the Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) [ 50 ]. Daily total fire hotspot counts were aggregated by subdivision.

Daily mean temperature and dew-point data were obtained from the ERA5-Land database [ 51 ]. Data were aggregated by subdivision. The daily relative humidity was derived from temperature and dew-point data [ 52 , 53 ].

The effects of extreme air pollution were investigated based on the haze and its conditions: (i) with or without fire activity and (ii) the duration of continuous haze days. Several sensitivity analyses were conducted to test the robustness of the main model. First, a different smoothing spline for temperature was applied—a natural cubic spline for moving average temperature lag 0–3 with three degrees of freedom (3 df). Second, we adjusted for relative humidity by using a natural cubic spline for moving average relative humidity lag 0–3 with 3 df. Third, different lag lengths were tested—lag 10, 14, and 21 days. Fourth, due to an apparent cluster of Puskesmas Bukit Rawi with the other puskesmas in Palangka Raya City, a sensitivity analysis was performed by grouping Puskesmas Bukit Rawi into Palangka Raya City (i.e. four puskesmas in Palangka Raya City, and two remaining in Pulang Pisau Regency). Finally, we tested the model without removing strata with zero cases.
Results:
During the study period, there were a total of 32 824 visits to puskesmas due to respiratory health outcomes, with daily average visits ranging from 1.8 ( Puskesmas Bukit Rawi) to 9.4 ( Puskesmas Menteng) cases ( Table 2 ). Of these, 71.4% were visits within Palangka Raya City. With variations across puskesmas , there were apparently higher trends of respiratory visits during July to October, and higher peaks especially in 2015 and 2019 ( Fig. 2A ). The daily average PM 10 concentration ranged from 66.1 to 86.1 μg/m 3 ( Table 3 ). There were two extreme peaks of PM 10 concentrations: one in 2015 (1303 μg/m 3 ) and another in 2019 (870 μg/m 3 ) ( Fig. 2B and C ).

The use of different haze definitions yielded different counts of total haze days and durations ( Table 3 ). There were more non-fire-haze days in Palangka Raya City (57.1%), but more fire-haze days in Pulang Pisau Regency (66.4%). Figure 2B and C demonstrates that most days with extremely high PM 10 concentrations in Pulang Pisau Regency were fire-haze days, whereas those observed in Palangka Raya City, including smaller peaks of PM 10 concentration, were mostly non-fire-haze days. The durations of fire-haze days were noticeably longer in Pulang Pisau Regency ( Table 3 and Fig. 2B and C ). When fire- or non-fire-haze days not specified, the longest duration of haze was observed in Puskesmas Bereng, located in Pulang Pisau Regency (75 days).

The effects of haze days on adverse respiratory outcomes appeared to differ in each subdivision by the haze definition used ( Fig. 3 ). The effects of haze days were pronounced in Pulang Pisau Regency, mainly contributed by fire haze. A null association was observed for the effects of haze days based on all three definitions in Palangka Raya City. Meanwhile, in Pulang Pisau Regency, haze days imposed an overall 36.6% [95% confidence interval (CI): 10.2%, 69.3%] increased risk of respiratory visits, with evidence observed for fire-haze days [74.4% (95% CI: 18.9%, 164.6%)] but not non-fire-haze days [26.3% (95% CI: –9.4%, 76.0%)]. There was no differential effect observed between a fire-haze and a non-fire-haze day.

Nonetheless, Fig. 4 shows that haze effects were sensitive to different definitions by duration. In Palangka Raya City, no haze effects were observed for short and moderate durations, but a reduced risk was observed when the haze duration was ≥15 days [–29.7% (95% CI: –43.9%, –11.7%)]. For Pulang Pisau Regency, prolonged durations were associated with an increased risk of respiratory visits. This pattern was clear when using both haze- and fire-haze-day definitions, with the highest risk observed when the duration of haze was ≥15 days [haze: 82.8% (95% CI: 31.7%, 153.7%); fire haze: 88.1% (95% CI: 13.8%, 210.8%)]. Although this pattern was observed for fire-haze days in Palangka Raya City, the effects were not significant. In both subdivisions, non-fire-haze days yielded non-significant associations, with apparently higher risk in Pulang Pisau Regency.

Different lag patterns of haze-related respiratory outcomes were observed in each subdivision, though evidence was weak ( Fig. 5 ). Non-fire haze followed an “n”-shaped lag pattern in both subdivisions, while the fire-haze lag pattern varied by location, with Pulang Pisau Regency showing a “u”-shaped lag pattern. The “n”-shaped lag pattern in Palangka Raya City was consistent for all-haze and non-fire-haze days when different durations were examined ( Supplementary Fig. S1a–c ). The lag patterns in Pulang Pisau Regency were also consistent throughout different durations.

When different lag lengths were tested, the risks remained only at shorter lags in Pulang Pisau Regency, while no changes were observed in Palangka Raya City ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Sensitivity analyses, which involved altering the lag structures for temperature, adjusting for relative humidity, modifying the puskesmas groupings, and without removing strata with zero cases, yielded consisted results, confirming the robustness of the main model ( Table 4 ).
Discussion:
Our study provides valuable insight into the respiratory health effects of smoke haze, with a focus on the presence of fire activities and haze duration in two subdivisions in Central Kalimantan (Palangka Raya City and Pulang Pisau Regency), Indonesia, from 2015 to 2019. The findings indicate that haze days pose a higher risk of adverse respiratory outcomes, consistently with a large body of epidemiological evidence [ 28 , 31 ], although some differences were noted when different haze definitions were used [ 28 ]. Haze characteristics, such as with or without local fire activities [ 42 ] and the duration of continuous occurrence [ 45 ], play an important role in elucidating the risk patterns. The risk of respiratory visits to puskesmas during smoke haze was prominent in Pulang Pisau Regency, which was mainly characterized by fire haze, but not in Palangka Raya City. With contrasting lag patterns, however, differential effects by fire- or non-fire haze remain inconclusive.

In Southeast Asia, haze can comprise both “fire” and “smoke” characteristics, hence different methods have been used when addressing its health effects [ 28 , 43 ]. We observed a pronounced risk of respiratory visits in Pulang Pisau Regency, especially on fire-haze days, but there was no significant difference between fire- and non-fire-haze days. This could be explained by the increased spread of haze-affected areas [ 34 ], the timing and severity of the burning [ 41 , 45 , 48 ], and the level of development of the subdivision [ 59 ]. When duration was considered, the pattern of increasing risk when the duration increased was observed for fire haze in both subdivisions. However, null associations were observed on haze days (Definition-1) with short and moderate durations in Palangka Raya City, while prolonged durations showed a reduced risk. If healthcare is assumed to have been equally accessible in both subdivisions during haze episodes, then this would affirm the idea that respiratory risk was higher in areas characterized by fire-haze days, which might potentially comprise different toxicities [ 25 ] and intensities [ 34 ] of pollutants.

It is also possible that healthcare access differed by area during haze periods, especially during prolonged and severe haze periods. Affected populations that encountered acute and severe health illnesses triggered during haze may have gone to hospitals instead of puskesmas , as essential medical resources are limited at puskesmas . According to one study, respiratory visits to primary healthcare centers increased during haze in urban/city areas, suggesting the possibility of better healthcare access in urban/city areas [ 59 ], consistently with the reduced risk observed over long durations of haze in Palangka Raya City. However, implementation of the national insurance policy in Indonesia since 2017 might have changed the population behavior, promoting visits to puskesmas under the subsidy, but this could not be explained by the previous study [ 59 ], which was conducted prior to 2017. Furthermore, better healthcare access in urban/city areas or unequally distributed health preventive measures may have led to the reduced risk during prolonged haze in Palangka Raya City. For example, during extreme haze, ‘ Posko Karhutla ’ is declared an affected area. Mobile clinics [“ Posyandu ” (“ Pos Pelayanan Terpadu ”), literally interpreted as ‘integrated service post’] are mobilized by the government as an extension of primary healthcare centers. In addition, oxygen houses are provided by the government and independent organizations. These may have resulted in a lower number of recorded puskesmas visits, though this cannot be confirmed in our study.

Haze characteristics should be considered while interpreting risk patterns over durations. Notably, fire haze exhibited increasing risk when the duration increased, as observed in both Palangka Raya City and Pulang Pisau Regency. For Pulang Pisau Regency, characterized by fire haze, haze (Definition-1) days exhibited the same ascending trend. However, fire-haze and non-fire-haze durations in Palangka Raya were short, suggesting that the longer duration of haze (Definition-1) was mainly contributed by a combination of short durations of both fire and non-fire haze ( Fig. 2B and C ). This may explain why a negative association was observed for long durations (≥15 days) of haze (Definition-1), resembling those of short-duration fire haze, even though a high risk with large uncertainty was observed for long-duration fire haze. Furthermore, haze characterized by fires demonstrated “u”-shaped lag patterns. Higher risks at shorter lags suggest the possibility of a trigger based on a sudden intense increase in air particles released from smoke or fires [ 48 ]. Meanwhile, the lowered risk in middle lags and higher risk in later lags could be explained as follows: first, residents may have taken preventive measures, such as reducing outdoor activities; second, puskesmas may have reached the daily capacity of visitors; and third, additional mobile clinics may have been set up temporarily during extreme haze. Nonetheless, there was no significant change in lag patterns over varying durations. More studies will be needed to clarify these relationships.

Smoke pollutants are potentially detrimental to respiratory outcomes, when they are both near [ 42 , 48 ] and distant [ 43 , 60 ] to the burning location, while toxicity depends on the burning conditions of underground peat [ 25 ]. Smoke pollutants remain detrimental even after being transported over distances [ 24 , 43 , 60 ]. Palangka Raya City is located downwind of Pulang Pisau Regency during the southwest monsoon, which is a dry season that favors fire ignitions and spread. As observed in our study, major haze episodes occurred during this monsoon season (July to September in 2015 and 2019). Therefore, the high PM 10 concentrations in Palangka Raya City may contain some transported pollutants from fires in upwind areas, playing a role in the notably high respiratory risk during haze days, independently of local fire activity. Consistently with this, Pulang Pisau Regency is a major burning area in Central Kalimantan [ 61 , 62 ], although burnings could be dominant in Palangka Raya City irregularly, particularly due to prescribed fires [ 63 ].

The use of primary healthcare visit data and the assessment of haze effects based on different characteristics offer crucial information to clarify the effects of haze on respiratory health in this region. Nonetheless, this study has several limitations. First, we could not ensure that all cases of adverse respiratory outcomes have been captured. This is due to two reasons: (i) only six puskesmas were included in this study due to the limitation of data availability and (ii) there was no information on the maximum visit capacity in puskesmas or on the number of cases in mobile clinics or hospitals. Second, it remains unclear whether there were any changes in puskesmas visits due to the implementation of the national insurance policy in 2017. Third, fire hotspot counts were used as a proxy for fire activity and to define fire-haze days. Exposure may have been attenuated if the fires had occurred in underground peat, which is not being captured in fire counts. However, our findings suggest no evidence of such differential effects. Haze by Definition-1, a more conservative definition, should always be examined.
Conclusion: The findings of this study suggest inconclusive effects of smoke haze on respiratory visits to primary healthcare centers. While strong evidence was observed in the area mainly characterized by fire haze, the varying risk patterns in different subdivisions and durations suggested the need for further investigation, with considerations of the haze characteristics.
